articles.title: Learning the Missing Derivative: Neural Multiple-Scattering Operators for Inverse Volume Rendering
articles.summary: Reconstructing optically thick media from photographs requires modeling multiple scattering and its response to changes in extinction. Frozen-source tomography discards this derivative; differentiable path tracing estimates it through expensive, noisy sampling. We instead predict the multiple-scattering field with a neural operator and differentiate through it during inverse rendering, while computing transmittance and single scattering directly. A further challenge arises during optimization: an operator that predicts the field accurately on held-out media can still produce poor derivatives at the density states visited by the optimizer. We address this by fine-tuning on states generated during inversions driven by the operator, using Monte Carlo scattering-field supervision. On held-out optically thick clouds, our method improves relighting over frozen-source tomography at equal time and outperforms differentiable path tracing given substantially more time. articles.title: From State of THE ART to Human Prediction Algorithms
articles.summary: Human curiosity and longing for the future have driven human progress from ancient times to the present. With the advancement of AI technology, human prediction algorithms have also drawn increasing attention from researchers. However, as AI technology continues to advance, we observe a counterintuitive phenomenon. Take human trajectory prediction algorithms as an example. Although models' quantitative prediction performance has improved, yielding one state-of-the-art model after another, the consideration of human behaviors, future thoughts, and social interactions themselves presents a gradually diminishing trend in the construction of these prediction algorithms, buried beneath numbers and metrics. In this manuscript, taking interactive art and human trajectory prediction algorithms as examples, we attempt to adopt a different analytical perspective to analyze the structural and developmental commonalities between these two fields. articles.title: Can an LVLM Perceive Event Boundaries Like a Human?
articles.summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) reason effectively about video content, but whether they perceive its event boundaries in a manner consistent with humans remains unclear. We first investigate this through Generic Event Boundary Detection (GEBD), which identifies event boundaries naturally perceived by humans in continuous video, without relying on predefined event categories. On Kinetics-GEBD dataset, LVLMs miss many boundaries when predicting directly from frames, but effectively refine candidates proposed by an unsupervised discovery method, achieving state-of-the-art unsupervised GEBD performance. We extend this discovery-refinement approach to hour-long egocentric video, where boundary discovery requires a broader semantic scale and whole-video LVLM refinement becomes impractical. articles.title: “Are You Sure?” Flipped Qwen2.5-1.5B’s Right Answer 2 Times in 3
articles.summary: Three small open models, 150 MMLU questions each, five pushback styles: “That’s wrong” did more damage, and naming a wrong option was close to fatal. The post “Are You Sure?” Flipped Qwen2.5-1.5B’s Right Answer 2 Times in 3 appeared first on Towards Data Science.

articles.title: UMAP 0.6: new initialization, new optimizers and faster performance [P]
articles.summary: UMAP 0.6 is out! A new initialization, new optimizers, and faster nearest neighbour search make UMAP much faster and far better at large scale. On 3 million arXiv papers it finishes in under 5 minutes, before UMAP 0.5 has even found its nearest neighbours. (race between UMAP0.5 and UMAP 0.6 video) Code: https://github.com/lmcinnes/umap Install: pip install -U umap-learn (also on conda-forge) Speed Neighbour search is ~4x faster by making better use of PyNNDescent. Initialization is faster with a new init method. With the new optimizers, the whole run is reproducible with a fixed seed while using every core. A seeded 0.5 run is single-threaded: 52 minutes, 12x longer. Quality Just as important as how quickly we get a result is the quality of the result. UMAP 0.6 works far better on million-scale datasets thanks to a new, better initialization and significant improvements in the optimizer.
